questions.title: How does the Cayley parameterization ensure the learned orthogonal matrix stays exactly orthogonal during BOFT training?
questions.question_body: In BOFT we define each butterfly component using a skew‑symmetric parameter ∫ such that R=(I+Q)(I−Q)^{-1}. I understand that if Q is skew‑symmetric then (I+Q)(I−Q)^{-1} is orthogonal, but could the Jacobian or numerical errors during back‑propagation cause the constraint to drift? How is orthogonality enforced in practice, and are there any stability tricks (e.g. re‑projection, step‑size restrictions) that the paper uses to keep ∫ in the skew‑symmetric manifold?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the 'minimum free edges' requirement in the information‑transmission framework?
questions.question_body: The paper states that each orthogonal factor must contain at least d edges to maintain full rank, and these edges are counted separately from trainable parameters because they are fixed to ±1. I’m puzzled: why can we consider those edges as ‘free’? Wouldn’t any non‑zero entry in a sparse orthogonal matrix still contribute to the parameter count if it is learnable? How does the authors’ counting of non‑zero edges reconcile with the usual parameter‑counting in sparse matrices?

questions.title: Why does a block‑diagonal orthogonal matrix fail to approximate classic linear transforms like the Fourier matrix?
questions.question_body: In the discussion on inductive bias, the authors claim that block‑diagonal OFT cannot recover any classic linear transform, whereas butterfly‑based BOFT can. Could you clarify mathematically why block‑diagonal structure prevents representing transforms that mix all input dimensions, while butterfly structure still allows global mixing?

questions.title: Can a single butterfly layer with ≥ 2b‑size blocks approximate any orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size and that by multiplying many butterfly matrices one can reach the full orthogonal group. Does this imply that a single butterfly matrix with block size b=2 (i.e. “2‑level” butterfly) already has universal expressivity if we allow enough layers m? If not, how many layers are theoretically required to approximate an arbitrary d×d orthogonal matrix, and how does this depend on the block size?

questions.title: Where does the -(b−1)dm/2 parameter count of BOFT come from?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BOFT(m,b) takes -(b−1)dm/2 effective trainable parameters for a d×n linear layer. I can follow that each 2b×2b butterfly block has (2b)²−b=3b²−b trainable entries (since a 2b×2b orthogonal matrix has b(2b−1) degrees of freedom). However, I am not sure how the product over m butterfly components and the block‑diagonal packing lead to the stated formula. Could you derive the parameter count step‑by‑step?

questions.title: How is multiplicative dropout implemented over butterfly components in practice?
questions.question_body: The authors introduce a multiplicative dropout that randomly replaces certain butterfly components or diagonal blocks with identity matrices. How is this selection done in code? Are the identities inserted as zeros in the skew‑symmetric parameter Q, or do we zero‑out the learned diagonal vectors d_i? Also, does this dropout affect the orthogonality of the overall product?

questions.title: What is the empirical trade‑off between block size b and depth m in BOFT?
questions.question_body: In the experiments, some configurations use small blocks (b=2) with large depth (m≈log d), achieving high parameter‑efficiency, while others use larger blocks with shallow depth. Could you explain any observed phenomena such as convergence speed, stability, or over‑fitting trends when varying b and m? Is there a practical guideline for choosing b and m for a new downstream task?

questions.title: How does BOFT handle non‑power‑of‑two model dimensions where d is not 2^N?
questions.question_body: The butterfly construction is defined recursively for d=2^N. Real‑world transformer layers often have hidden dimensions like 768 or 1024, which are not exact powers of two. Does the paper pad the matrices to the next power‑of‑two, use an additional projection layer, or adjust the butterfly structure somehow? What are the implications for parameter count and approximation error?

questions.title: What would happen if we replace the butterfly pattern with another sparse network topology, e.g. a torus or hypercube?
questions.question_body: The information‑transmission framework suggests that any directed graph with dense end‑to‑end connectivity could serve as a factorization pattern. If we use a different topology that still has <d log d edges, could we gain better expressivity or training speed? Why did the authors choose the butterfly specifically, and are there known bounds on the minimal number of edges required for a fully connected d→d linear transform?

questions.title: Can BOFT be combined with LoRA or other low‑rank adaptations for even greater efficiency?
questions.question_body: Since LoRA adds a low‑rank update of the form WA+VB^T, and BOFT multiplies the weight by an orthogonal matrix, it seems possible to apply both simultaneously. Would such a hybrid model benefit from both sparsity and low‑rank structure, and how would the joint optimization be formulated given the different parameter‑count and regularization effects?
